parts.note: taken as written
trials are tests

explanation.surface: A witness speaks up in court during a series of trials.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trials' reads as court cases, but here they are tests, as in experiments.
explanation.definitionFit: To give evidence is to bear witness, or vouch, that something is true.

clue.text: Sticks the notices round this place

indicators.note: round says the first piece goes about the second

parts.note: ADS, advertisements, are notices
this place is here

explanation.surface: Posters are pasted up all around here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the notices' are advertisements, shortened as is usual; 'this place' is simply here.
explanation.definitionFit: To adhere is to cling or remain fixed, a synonym for sticks.

indicators.note: when loud says the word is spoken aloud, so its sound counts

parts.note: someone who gets bored tires of something

explanation.surface: Bells sound, and someone grows weary of the noise.
explanation.walkthrough: TIRES, gets bored, said aloud matches TYRES; 'Rings' reads as bells but means the circular rubber wheels.
explanation.definitionFit: Tyres are the rubber hoops fitted on wheels, ring shapes in form.

clue.text: Her best formula for effervescent powder

indicators.note: a formula is a mix or recipe, telling you to remix the letters

explanation.surface: A woman's finest recipe for a fizzy sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'formula' asks for the letters of HER BEST to be rearranged; sherbet in Britain is a fizzy sweet powder.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherbet is a sweet powder that fizzes on the tongue, a British children's sweet.

clue.text: Left out fruit cake — was pilfered

indicators.note: out says the piece named is to be left out of the word

parts.note: stollen is a German fruit cake

explanation.surface: Someone excluded from the fruit cake took some anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' takes L out of STOLLEN, a German Christmas fruit loaf; 'was' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something taken by petty theft has been stolen.

indicators.note: making here means fashioning the letters of the next word into something new

explanation.surface: A rope fibre suited to the manufacture of a ship's canvas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making' asks for the letters of SAILS to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Sisal is a stiff plant fibre from an agave, used for rope and twine.

indicators.note: in places the first piece inside the hut word

parts.note: a shed is a hut
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone flinched on being inside a hut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one's in hut' reads as one is in hut: I goes inside SHED.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse that shies jumps back in fright, so it has recoiled.

clue.text: Leave port, after drunken siesta get lost

indicators.note: after says the next piece follows the one before
drunken suggests the letters of the next word stagger into a new order

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for lost, as in sports tables

explanation.surface: A sailor sets off after a boozy nap and goes missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get' is only a link word; L for lost is the abbreviation used in sports league tables.
explanation.definitionFit: To set sail is to begin a sea voyage, departing from harbour.

clue.text: Promise to remove piano from shelf

indicators.note: to remove says the named letter is taken away from the word

parts.note: a pledge is a promise
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

explanation.surface: Someone vows to shift a piano off a shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to remove' takes P (piano, the musical direction for soft) from PLEDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A ledge is a narrow shelf jutting from a wall or rock face.

indicators.note: coming round suggests the letters of the next word turn about into a new order

explanation.surface: A creature wanders along the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes round' tells you to rearrange the letters of SHORE.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse is one example of a large four-legged beast.

indicators.note: about here means the letters of the following words are moved around

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether Em was passed over, and the same for another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' asks for the letters of EM and DITTO, together, to be rearranged; the question mark and full stop are only surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To skip something is to leave it out, the same sense as missed out.

indicators.note: among says the letters lie within the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Someone admits they scattered rubbish, a ridiculous thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' points into 'debris, I blew', where the letters run across all three words, ignoring the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: Something laughable is ridiculous, so the two words are synonyms.

indicators.note: rearranged plainly says the letters of the priest's title go in another order

explanation.surface: A chaplain moved the curtains around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rearranged' asks for the letters of PADRE to be shuffled; a padre is a military chaplain.
explanation.definitionFit: A drape is a heavy hanging cloth, a synonym for a curtain, especially in American usage.

indicators.note: in says one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: something glittering is shiny

indicators.note: ending picks out only the final letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A sudden finish to a dazzling sporting event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ending' gives T, the last letter of 'Abrupt', which goes 'in' SHINY. Shinty is a Scottish stick-and-ball game rather like hockey.
explanation.definitionFit: Shinty is a team game played with curved sticks, an example of a sport from the Scottish Highlands.

parts.note: IN means fashionable or popular
a sip is a small drink
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: A fashionable drink I had tasted of nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I had' contracts to I'D.
explanation.definitionFit: Insipid food lacks taste, so it is bland.

parts.note: S is the usual abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
leanings are inclinations or tilts

explanation.surface: Slight inclinations toward the big top's equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leanings' reads as preferences, but it means physical tilts; 'towards' just links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Stilts are tall poles a performer walks on, typical equipment at a circus.

indicators.note: over in a down clue means the word is turned upside down, read back

parts.note: met means encountered

indicators.note: false says the letters of the following word are not in their true order

explanation.surface: A storm struck after a misstep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns MET to TEM; 'false' rearranges STEP to PEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A tempest is a violent windstorm, a literary synonym.

clue.text: Shed loses end with explosive noise, the whole thing!

indicators.note: loses end means the last letter of the word drops off

parts.note: a bang is an explosive noise

explanation.surface: A shed collapses with a loud blast, the entire structure gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses end' cuts D from SHED, leaving SHE; 'with' links to BANG.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom the whole shebang means everything, the entire affair.

clue.text: River always enclosed by two points

indicators.note: enclosed by means the first piece surrounds the second

parts.note: S and N are two compass points, south and north
ever means always

explanation.surface: A river that is forever hemmed in by two headlands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enclosed by' puts EVER between S and N, compass points. The Severn is Britain's longest river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Severn is the longest river in Britain, flowing through Wales and England.

clue.text: Sat with head of paper, very big editor

indicators.note: head of takes only the leading letter of the following word

parts.note: OS stands for outsize, a clothing label for very big

explanation.surface: A newspaper's huge editor sat for a portrait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head of' gives P from 'paper'; OS is the clothing label for outsize.
explanation.definitionFit: To pose is to sit for a portrait or photograph, holding still for the artist.

clue.text: Complicated plot about a Greek philosopher

indicators.note: about says the rearranged letters go round the small word
complicated suggests the letters of the next word are tangled into a new order

explanation.surface: An intricate story concerning a thinker from Athens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complicated' rearranges PLOT to PLTO; 'about' puts it round A.
explanation.definitionFit: Plato was a pupil of Socrates and one of the founders of Western philosophy.

indicators.note: in says the pieces go inside the word for boring

parts.note: something dull is dry
I is the Roman numeral for one
A is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: One item in a tedious magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts I and A inside DRY.
explanation.definitionFit: A diary is a daily written record, a personal journal.

clue.text: Then Ma's sent round as a group

indicators.note: round here means the surrounding words enclose the letters sought

explanation.surface: Mother has dispatched someone, and they all went together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' says the outer words wrap round the run: thEN MA'S SEnt, ignoring the apostrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means all together, in one body, the same as collectively.

clue.text: Like the Doctor Who series, if CSI takes a turn

indicators.note: takes a turn means the letters spin round into another order

explanation.surface: A crime show changes direction and becomes like a time-travel drama.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes a turn' rearranges IF CSI; Doctor Who is the long-running British science-fiction TV series, and CSI an American crime drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctor Who is a time-travel drama, belonging to the science-fiction genre.

indicators.note: consuming means one piece swallows the other, so it goes inside

parts.note: an ape is a primate, loosely a monkey
peas are green vegetables

explanation.surface: A monkey is kept happy by eating its vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: 'greens' looks like a colour, but means green vegetables; an ape is loosely called a monkey.
explanation.definitionFit: To appease someone is to pacify or placate them, meeting their demands.

clue.text: Heather seen when morning departs the USA

indicators.note: departs means the named piece leaves the longer word

parts.note: the USA is America
AM is the abbreviation for morning, ante meridiem

explanation.surface: A woman called Heather is spotted leaving the United States one morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heather' looks like a woman's name, but it is the plant; 'departs' takes AM out of AMERICA.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is the botanical genus of heaths, so the plant shares its name.

clue.text: Not even lady rejects commercial, strangely

parts.note: a number that is not even is odd

indicators.note: rejects says the named piece is thrown out of the word

parts.note: taken as written before the deletion
AD is short for advertisement, a commercial

explanation.surface: A woman with a peculiar dislike of TV adverts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejects' removes AD from LADY, leaving LY.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean in a peculiar or unusual way.

explanation.surface: Seizing hold of a rope tied in knots.
explanation.definitionFit: Catching fish or animals in a mesh is snaring them, and a mesh of knotted cord or rope is the material of a net.
